description: We are a dedicated team of physics enthusiasts passionate about space exploration and Earth observation data. Our team brings together skills in Python programming, physics modeling, data analysis, and UI/UX design. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we are creating a digital mapping tool to identify ground sites that reflect conditions of bases on the Moon and Mars.
summary:
Surface Sync is an analytical web platform designed to automatically identify and match planetary analogs across Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Developing rovers, spacesuits, and life-support systems requires rigorous testing in harsh extraterrestrial environments - a process that can cost billions of dollars during actual space missions. Surface Sync addresses this challenge through a unique, bidirectional search capability: users can select any point on an interactive map or enter specific coordinates to perform real-time analysis.
By selecting a location on Earth, engineers can instantly identify analogous sites on the Moon and Mars, which aids in selecting locations for future stations and bases. Conversely, by selecting an extraterrestrial site, the system finds a corresponding location on Earth, facilitating the testing of equipment. The platform also enables the identification of Martian-like terrain on the Moon, and vice versa. This is of immense value to space exploration, as it provides researchers and engineers with natural testing grounds. Furthermore, the ability to locate Earth-like environments on other planets is critical for planning future expeditions, conducting scientific research, and identifying suitable sites for the construction of bases and stations.
details:
Users can select any point on an interactive map or enter specific coordinates, triggering a multi-layered analytical engine that evaluates the chosen area based on a comprehensive seven-layer profile. The system simultaneously processes seven key geophysical and scientific parameters: Layer 1 (NASA PDS - MGS MOLA) assesses topography, elevation, slope steepness, surface irregularities, craters, and other surface features; Layer 2 (NASA PDS - MGS TES / MCS) analyzes temperature, illumination levels, and extreme environmental conditions; Layer 3 (NASA PDS - MGS TES / MCS) evaluates the presence of water, ice, permafrost, and other potential resources; Layer 4 (NASA PDS - MGS TES / MCS) examines dust factors, wind activity, erosion, and other atmospheric or surface processes; Layer 5 (an astrobiological model) investigates biological aspects, extremophiles, habitability, and biosignatures; Layer 6 (NASA PDS - MRO CRISM / SHARAD) scans the surface for caves, lava tubes, subsurface voids, and other underground structures; and Layer 7 (a NASA engineering index) assesses conditions critical for landing, mobility, navigation, robotic operations, crewed expeditions, or construction.

To process vast orbital datasets directly within a browser - eliminating the need for heavy GIS software or large amounts of local storage - the platform employs an optimized client-side loading and computation engine. Upon the selection of coordinates, the application generates a multidimensional digital profile of the site by dynamically querying open scientific APIs and pre-calibrated planetary models. The system retrieves terrain data from NASA Trek (LRO LOLA, MGS MOLA, and SRTM), climate metrics from the NASA POWER API, current meteorological information from Open-Meteo, lithological data from the Macrostrat API, and thermal characteristic data from LRO Diviner, MRO, and Mars Express. An algorithm then scans the target planetary surface area using a grid, calculating parameter deviations across seven distinct layers. Based on this, the system computes similarity scores for each layer, along with a final weighted correspondence coefficient, enabling it to identify the six most accurate planetary analogs. The platform’s primary advantage lies in its real-time, bidirectional search architecture, which does not rely on static, pre-compiled databases. Its flexible operational mechanism - unconstrained by rigid, fixed parameters - offers exceptional versatility. Engineers can select a location on Earth and find its analogs on Mars or the Moon - for instance, to identify sites suitable for constructing future bases or stations. Conversely, one can specify a particular region or landscape type on Mars or the Moon to locate an Earth-based analog, serving as a natural testing ground for planetary rovers and equipment; the system can also identify analogs for lunar terrain on Mars, and vice versa.

The goal of the Surface Sync project is to significantly reduce the multi-billion-dollar costs and logistical risks associated with preparing for extraterrestrial missions. By accelerating the search for Earth-based analogs and enabling precise, multifactorial modeling of alien environments, the platform makes planetary exploration more accessible and optimizes the strategic planning of future expeditions to the Moon and Mars.

The application was developed using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, integrated with the Leaflet.js mapping engine. It connects complex streams of orbital data to a user-friendly web interface hosted on GitHub and Vercel. The project offers a fundamentally new approach: the search for planetary analogs is transformed from a labor-intensive process of manually reviewing scientific literature into an instantaneous, interactive exploration. Throughout development, the team prioritized scientific accuracy, high computational speed, and user-friendliness. They reconciled disparate coordinate systems and spatial resolutions, established weighting coefficients for seven geophysical parameters - while accounting for practical engineering constraints - and optimized the scanning speed across the global data grid. This enabled the conversion of orbital telemetry into clear, actionable metrics for assessing the similarity between objects.
